cards.title: Decision versus approximate counting for fixed-width SAT
cards.formal: For every fixed clause width \(k\geq3\), do randomized decision \(k\)-SAT and randomized multiplicative approximation of \(\#k\)-SAT have the same optimal exponential running-time rate in the number of variables? With \(d_k\) and \(a_k\) defined below, the target is \(a_k=d_k\) for every fixed \(k\geq3\). This makes “close the gap” precise at the exponential-rate level, as in the later source’s fixed-width question.
cards.why: Tests whether estimating the number of satisfying assignments intrinsically requires more exponential work than finding out whether any exist. Equality would transfer the leading exponential savings in fixed-width SAT to a broader counting task.
cards.status_note: Read the original approximation convention and question, the 2013 authors’ reported improvement, and the full November 2020 author version of the 2021 journal paper, especially its explicit fixed-width question and Theorem 13. Later-result searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The chosen target is equality of infimum exponential rates with polynomial accuracy cost, not a requirement of polynomial-overhead reduction or identical lower-order running time.

cards.definitions:
An input is a Boolean CNF formula \(F\) on an explicitly declared set of \(n\) variables, with at most \(k\) literals in each clause. A literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(N(F)\) be the number of assignments to all declared variables satisfying every clause. Variables absent from clauses still contribute their two possible values. There is no promise of satisfiability or sparsity.

Decision asks whether \(N(F)>0\). Approximate counting receives a rational accuracy parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and must output a nonnegative binary-encoded rational \(Z\) such that
\[
(1-\varepsilon)N(F)\leq Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)N(F)
\]
with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. When \(N(F)=0\), a successful output is exactly zero. Probability is over algorithmic randomness. Decision also has success probability at least \(2/3\), allowing two-sided error.

Use ordinary classical randomized algorithms and worst-case bit-operation running time, over both inputs and random tapes. Let \(L\) be total input bit length, including the formula and, for approximate counting, the rational accuracy. Define \(d_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which decision has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}L^C)\) for some fixed \(C\). Define \(a_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which an approximation scheme has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}(L+\varepsilon^{-1})^C)\) for some fixed \(C\), for every admissible accuracy. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and hidden constants may depend on the fixed \(k\) and \(\alpha\), but not on the input or accuracy.

The infima need not be attained. Equality asks that every exponential decision rate can be matched for approximation with any arbitrarily small positive addition to that rate and polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy. It does not demand a single optimal algorithm at an unattained infimum, identical polynomial factors, or an effective compiler transforming all decision programs.

Already \(d_k\leq a_k\): a constant-relative-error estimate distinguishes zero from a positive count. The unresolved direction compares approximation with decision at the same fixed clause width. Taking a supremum or a limit over all widths is a different statement. A reduction whose decision queries add parity constraints or increase clause width must account for their cost before it can establish this comparison. The source uses an \(e^\varepsilon\) multiplicative convention; changing to the displayed relative-error convention only rescales accuracy by constant factors in this range.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove equality of the two defined infimum rates for every fixed integer width at least three, or prove a strict separation for at least one such width. A reduction preserving the width and adding arbitrarily small exponential overhead would suffice for equality. Improved individual upper bounds, a result only as width tends to infinity, or hardness for exact counting alone does not settle this comparison.

context_blocks.title: Approximation improved before the gap closed
context_blocks.text: Thurley obtains a randomized approximation scheme substantially faster than the exact counting bounds cited in 2012. Schmitt and Wanka later improve the three-literal upper bound to \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}1.51426^n)\). These are historical upper bounds, not claims about the optimal rates or the latest decision record.

context_blocks.title: Later reductions preserve all-width savings
context_blocks.text: Dell and Lapinskas show that a common exponential saving for decision at every constant width transfers to approximate counting with arbitrarily small loss. Their Theorem 8 therefore matches the all-width saving, but its hypothesis is stronger than having a fast algorithm at one selected width.

context_blocks.title: The same-width question remains distinct
context_blocks.text: The full journal version explicitly leaves the fixed-width exponential comparison open. Its main SAT reduction uses a decision problem with sparse parity constraints; encoding those constraints into CNF may require larger width. It also relates subexponential decision and approximation, without settling each fixed positive exponential rate.

cards.context:

Schmitt and Wanka later improve the three-literal upper bound to \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}1.51426^n)\). These are historical upper bounds, not claims about the optimal rates or the latest decision record.

Dell and Lapinskas show that a common exponential saving for decision at every constant width transfers to approximate counting with arbitrarily small loss. Their Theorem 8 therefore matches the all-width saving, but its hypothesis is stronger than having a fast algorithm at one selected width.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
